## Overview

In this lab, you will:

1. Scrape the 2026 Hall of Fame voting results
2. Clean and reformat the data
3. Compare the scraped data to the `HallOfFame` table in the `Lahman` package
4. Save the updated dataset to a `csv` file
5. Document the process

<br><br>

The deliverables are:

* Your individual `R` script in the team repo (one per team member)
    + Commenting is part of this!
* Final `csv` (one per team)
* Updated README to answer questions


## Data Background

### Lahman Data Package
The Lahman data package is based on [Sean Lahman](https://www.seanlahman.com/)'s  Baseball [Database](https://sabr.org/lahman-database/).

The `HallOfFame` table does contain some Hall of Fame data for 2026. You can compare your scraped data with the 2026 data to see what matches and what does not match.


### Baseball Reference

The site baseball-reference.com has grown out of Sean Lahman's work and is now maintained independently. It also has tables with Hall of Fame information, e.g., for 2026:

[https://www.baseball-reference.com/awards/hof_2026.shtml](https://www.baseball-reference.com/awards/hof_2026.shtml)


### Important note!

The Baseball Reference page and the Lahman `HallOfFame` table do not have to match row-for-row.

Baseball Reference shows the full BBWAA ballot for 2026.

The Lahman `HallOfFame` table stores official Hall of Fame voting records in a different format, and it may include different voting bodies.

This means that your scraped data may have more rows than the Lahman data for 2026.

That is okay.

Part of the goal is to understand how the two data sources are structured and where they differ.


## Process

### Step 1: Create your own R script

1. Accept the link to Classroom 50 on the Canvas Lab #4 assignment
2. Since you are working in your final project teams, we have set up your teams for you already. Once one person has accepted, the repo will populate.
3. Clone the repo to your local session (see below for Positron steps).
4. Each person should make their own `R` script titled `progress_report_<your name>.R`. For example, mine would be `progress_report_jennifer_daddysman.R`. 
5. Copy the information from the `progress_report_template.R` script into the file you have created and save this to your repo.
6. Commit the file and push.


### Step 2: Scrape the data

The following packages should already be in your R script. Feel free to add other packages as you see fit.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(Lahman)
```

Steps:

1. Use the `rvest` package to read the table of Hall of Fame voting results for 2026 from [https://www.baseball-reference.com/awards/hof_2026.shtml](https://www.baseball-reference.com/awards/hof_2026.shtml).
2. Store the scraped data in a data frame called `hall2026`.

**Note:** Be polite! Only scrape the data once. Don't run your whole R script; only run the sections that you currently need.


### Step 3: Clean the data

What steps are necessary to get the scraped data into a useful format? You should think about questions such as:

1. Are the variable names correct?
2. Which columns do you want to keep?
3. Which variables should be numeric?
4. How can you identify who was inducted?

Document your process in your section of the `README.md` file and in your code comments in your R script.


### Step 4: Compare to Lahman

The Lahman data can help us understand what information is stored in the `HallOfFame` table:

```{r}
HallOfFame |>
    filter(yearID == 2026)
```

Compare your scraped data to the Lahman data.

(Potential) questions to think about and to document in your code comments and your section of the `README.md`:

1. How many rows are in your scraped data?
2. How many are in the Lahman dataset for 2026?
3. Why might these numbers be different?
4. Which players were inducted according to the BBWAA table?
5. Are the same players represented in Lahman? 


### Step 5: Save the dataset

Each team member should create a cleaned Hall of Fame voting dataset for the year 2026. Compare your results and, as a team, select one as your final result. Describe why you made the choice you did in the `README.md`.

Your final dataset should include the cleaned version of the Baseball Reference Hall of Fame data (scraped data). **At a minimum**, the `csv` should include the following:

1. candidate name
2. year
3. votes (number player received)
4. ballots (total number of ballots)
5. needed (number of votes needed)
6. percent of vote
7. whether the candidate was inducted

Your final data may include more columns.


### Step 6: Submission

1. Each individual: Push changes to your file `progress_report_<your name>.R` to the repo. We will check the commit history and in-file comments for grading.
2. Each individual: Make sure your process for Steps 3 and 4 is documented in the `README.md` file (pushed successfully).
3. As a team: Push one final `csv` meeting the above requirements to the repo. Include your reasoning in the `README.md`.

## Some Data Wrangling/Tidying Tricks

### Variable names in line 1

Obtain the column names from the first line as a variable. Overwrite the column names with the actual column names. Then delete the first line:

```{r}
#| eval: false
data <- tables[[1]]
actual_col_names <- data[1, ]
colnames(data) <- actual_col_names
data <- data[-1, ]
```


### Character to numeric

Make sure all numeric variables are saved as numeric. The code below is just an example:

```{r}
#| eval: false
data$Votes <- as.numeric(data$Votes)
data$percent_vote <- readr::parse_number(data$`%vote`)
```

### Using `gsub`

`gsub(pattern, replacement, x)`:  replace all occurrences of `pattern` in vector `x` by the string `replacement`.

```{r}
x <- c("David Ortiz", "X-Barry Bonds", "X-Roger Clemens")

gsub("X-", "Oh no! ", x)

gsub("X-", "", x)
```


### Combining datasets with the same variables

If two data frames have the same variable names, we can use the command **`rbind`** (row bind) to concatenate them.

```{r}
#| eval: false
x1 <- data.frame(id=1:2, name=c("A", "B"))
x2 <- data.frame(id=3:4, name=c("C", "D"))
dframe <- rbind(x1, x2)
```

Don't forget to save the result!


### Exporting `csv` files

**`write.csv`** writes a data frame into a comma-separated values file (extension csv):

```{r}
#| eval: false
write.csv(dframe, file="some-file.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Make sure to not export the row names, otherwise each successive read & write of the file adds another column in the front.


**`write_csv`** is not part of base, but faster, and does not convert special characters into `.`

```{r}
#| eval: false
readr::write_csv(dframe, file="some-other-file.csv")
```
